extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset comprised of images depicting complex everyday scenes of common objects in their natural context, containing 91 common object types with 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization and scene understanding.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.isLiveDataset: MS COCO will evolve and grow over time; up to date information is available online.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Candidate images were collected from Flickr by searching for pairwise combinations of object categories, scene/object category pairs, and single categories with an explicit filtering stage to harvest non-iconic images with contextual relationships. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Photographs uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords on Flickr.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Removal of near-duplicate images using GIST descriptors, grouping images by photographer and date taken across dataset splits, and human filtering on Amazon Mechanical Turk to remove invalid or iconic images.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdsourced pipeline consisting of: 1) Category labeling using a hierarchical approach with 11 super-categories where workers dragged icons onto an instance; 2) Instance spotting where workers marked up to 10 instances of a specified category with crosses using a magnifying glass; 3) Instance segmentation where workers traced object boundaries using a modified OpenSurfaces interface following a training task, or painted 'crowd' regions for images with more than 10-15 instances; 4) Segmentation verification where workers judged segmentation quality; and 5) Adding five written caption descriptions per image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For category labeling, worker quality was evaluated against expert workers; union of 8 AMT workers achieved over 99% recall. Precision and recall were analyzed via leave-one-out evaluation, and workers below a precision threshold had their work rejected. In segmentation verification, 3 to 5 workers judged each mask, and instances not receiving at least 4 out of 5 favorable votes were discarded and re-annotated. Segmentations from workers who consistently produced poor quality were discarded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers per image for category labeling; 8 workers per image for instance spotting; 1 worker per instance for instance segmentation; 3 to 5 workers per instance for segmentation verification; 5 written caption descriptions per image.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Split into two releases: 2014 release (82,783 train, 40,504 val, and 40,775 test images with 80 categories) and cumulative 2015 release (165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images across 91 categories). Train and validation annotations are released, test annotations are held out for an automatic evaluation server.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Discussion of iconic vs. non-iconic image biases; the dataset explicitly targets non-canonical viewpoints, occlusion, and clutter rather than iconic, centered images. It also notes the long tail phenomenon in natural object frequency distributions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: 11 categories were omitted from segmentation in the initial 2014 release due to too many instances (hat, shoe, eyeglasses), ambiguity/difficulty (mirror, window, door, street sign), confusion (plate, desk), or too few instances (blender, hair brush). Dense groupings exceeding 10-15 instances were marked as crowd segments rather than individually segmented. Labeling is limited to 'thing' categories without 'stuff' categories.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, testing, and benchmarking models for object recognition, bounding-box detection, instance-level segmentation, contextual reasoning, and scene understanding.
